Name: Description | Small scale, subsistence farmers: The population of the region is largely rural and dependent on subsistence farming as their principal livelihood. According to the  ILO  census  of  2001,  the  population  of  the  Alaotra  Mangoro  Region  was  978,272,  of  which  82%  were  rural.  Slash-and-burn  agriculture  –  called  Tavy  –  is  a  traditional  technique  favoured  by  the  people  of  the  region.  Some  farmers may  practice  Tavy  exclusively. The primary crop in  Tavy is rice, often  with cassava,  or vegetables. A common scenario is for a  Tavy farmer on  steep  slopes  to  plant  rice  for  a  couple  of  years,  then,  as  soil  nutrient  concentrations  drop,  shift  to  cassava.  As  nutrients  are  depleted further, the land may be left in fallow for a number of years and returned to another round of production, this time at  lower  yields.  On  moderate  slopes,  Tavy  yields  may  diminish  by  50%  after  3  years  of  cultivation,  and  on  steep  slopes  Tavy  yields may fall by 50% within two years (Styger et al. 2007). When land is in short supply, the fallow period is reduced, and the  soil is rapidly degraded. At some point the land may be used for grazing or similar low-productivity use, or it may be cropped  continuously until it is exhausted and abandoned, and the Tavy farmer may look for more forest to repeat the process.  Tavy  farmers,  working  on  high,  steep,  remote  hills,  tend  to  be  isolated  from  large  villages  and  markets,  so  grow  crops  for  subsistence, primarily rice and cassava. Especially in isolated areas with limited markets, crops are grown in accordance with a  concept  of  requirements.  A  farmer  practicing  Tavy  will  farm  as  long  as  necessary  to  grow  a  certain  amount  of  food  for  household consumption and limited trade, and not necessarily more.  Soil nutrients generally decline in Tavy lands under cultivation. Studying plots in eastern Madagascar, Brand (Brand and Pfund  1998) showed that soils planted in an upland rice-fallow system show declining concentrations of nutrients. In long-term shifting  cultivation, the soil nutrient stock may fall by a third, and over a longer period of intensive use, the soil may lose more than 90%  of the nutrient concentration of soils in rainforest, and support only grass. Recovery of nutrients in fallow upland is very  slow,  starting to increase after 3-5 years of fallow (Brand and Pfund 1998).

Name: Description | Small scale, subsistence farmers: The population of the region is largely rural and dependent on subsistence farming as their principal livelihood. According to the  ILO  census  of  2001,  the  population  of  the  Alaotra  Mangoro  Region  was  978,272,  of  which  82%  were  rural.  Slash-and-burn  agriculture  –  called  Tavy  –  is  a  traditional  technique  favoured  by  the  people  of  the  region.  Some  farmers may  practice  Tavy  exclusively. The primary crop in  Tavy is rice, often  with cassava,  or vegetables. A common scenario is for a  Tavy farmer on  steep  slopes  to  plant  rice  for  a  couple  of  years,  then,  as  soil  nutrient  concentrations  drop,  shift  to  cassava.  As  nutrients  are  depleted further, the land may be left in fallow for a number of years and returned to another round of production, this time at  lower  yields.  On  moderate  slopes,  Tavy  yields  may  diminish  by  50%  after  3  years  of  cultivation,  and  on  steep  slopes  Tavy  yields may fall by 50% within two years (Styger et al. 2007). When land is in short supply, the fallow period is reduced, and the  soil is rapidly degraded. At some point the land may be used for grazing or similar low-productivity use, or it may be cropped  continuously until it is exhausted and abandoned, and the Tavy farmer may look for more forest to repeat the process.  Tavy  farmers,  working  on  high,  steep,  remote  hills,  tend  to  be  isolated  from  large  villages  and  markets,  so  grow  crops  for  subsistence, primarily rice and cassava. Especially in isolated areas with limited markets, crops are grown in accordance with a  concept  of  requirements.  A  farmer  practicing  Tavy  will  farm  as  long  as  necessary  to  grow  a  certain  amount  of  food  for  household consumption and limited trade, and not necessarily more.  Soil nutrients generally decline in Tavy lands under cultivation. Studying plots in eastern Madagascar, Brand (Brand and Pfund  1998) showed that soils planted in an upland rice-fallow system show declining concentrations of nutrients. In long-term shifting  cultivation, the soil nutrient stock may fall by a third, and over a longer period of intensive use, the soil may lose more than 90%  of the nutrient concentration of soils in rainforest, and support only grass. Recovery of nutrients in fallow upland is very  slow,  starting to increase after 3-5 years of fallow (Brand and Pfund 1998).

Name: Description | Small scale, subsistence farmers: The population of the region is largely rural and dependent on subsistence farming as their principal livelihood. According to the  ILO  census  of  2001,  the  population  of  the  Alaotra  Mangoro  Region  was  978,272,  of  which  82%  were  rural.  Slash-and-burn  agriculture  –  called  Tavy  –  is  a  traditional  technique  favoured  by  the  people  of  the  region.  Some  farmers may  practice  Tavy  exclusively. The primary crop in  Tavy is rice, often  with cassava,  or vegetables. A common scenario is for a  Tavy farmer on  steep  slopes  to  plant  rice  for  a  couple  of  years,  then,  as  soil  nutrient  concentrations  drop,  shift  to  cassava.  As  nutrients  are  depleted further, the land may be left in fallow for a number of years and returned to another round of production, this time at  lower  yields.  On  moderate  slopes,  Tavy  yields  may  diminish  by  50%  after  3  years  of  cultivation,  and  on  steep  slopes  Tavy  yields may fall by 50% within two years (Styger et al. 2007). When land is in short supply, the fallow period is reduced, and the  soil is rapidly degraded. At some point the land may be used for grazing or similar low-productivity use, or it may be cropped  continuously until it is exhausted and abandoned, and the Tavy farmer may look for more forest to repeat the process.  Tavy  farmers,  working  on  high,  steep,  remote  hills,  tend  to  be  isolated  from  large  villages  and  markets,  so  grow  crops  for  subsistence, primarily rice and cassava. Especially in isolated areas with limited markets, crops are grown in accordance with a  concept  of  requirements.  A  farmer  practicing  Tavy  will  farm  as  long  as  necessary  to  grow  a  certain  amount  of  food  for  household consumption and limited trade, and not necessarily more.  Soil nutrients generally decline in Tavy lands under cultivation. Studying plots in eastern Madagascar, Brand (Brand and Pfund  1998) showed that soils planted in an upland rice-fallow system show declining concentrations of nutrients. In long-term shifting  cultivation, the soil nutrient stock may fall by a third, and over a longer period of intensive use, the soil may lose more than 90%  of the nutrient concentration of soils in rainforest, and support only grass. Recovery of nutrients in fallow upland is very  slow,  starting to increase after 3-5 years of fallow (Brand and Pfund 1998).
